title: Local Excitation, Global Inhibition
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter reviews the local-excitation, global-inhibition (LEGI) reaction–diffusion model for biological pattern formation — a Turing-type activator–inhibitor system — carrying the analysis from the two reaction–diffusion equations through the nondimensionalized system, the spatially uniform steady state, and the stability of that steady state, up to the point where the notes introduce a spatially varying perturbation. It assumes the reader already has reaction–diffusion equations, linearizing a nonlinear system around a fixed point, and the trace/determinant test for stability of a two-variable linear system. The source is explicitly titled "Review," jumps straight into equations with no restated motivation, and presumes that setup was built in an earlier lecture — one not among the inputs supplied for this chapter. The supplied material is short and, in places, garbled by the PDF-to-text conversion; it also breaks off mid-derivation before reaching the actual instability condition. This chapter goes exactly as far as the material does and says plainly where it stops. ## The model: an activator and an inhibitor, reacting and diffusing The system tracks two chemical species varying in one spatial dimension: an activator $a(x,t)$ and an inhibitor $i(x,t)$, obeying $$\frac{\partial a}{\partial t} = r_a + k_a \frac{a^2}{i} - \gamma_a a + D_a \frac{\partial^2 a}{\partial x^2}, \qquad \frac{\partial i}{\partial t} = k_i a^2 - \gamma_i i + D_i \frac{\partial^2 i}{\partial x^2}.$$ The variables are $a$, $i$ (the two concentrations), $t$ (time), and $x$ (position). The constants are $r_a$ (a basal activator synthesis rate), $k_a, k_i$ (synthesis rate constants), $\gamma_a, \gamma_i$ (decay rates), and $D_a, D_i$ (diffusion constants). Reading the two equations off directly: the activator autocatalyses through the $a^2/i$ term, but that term is suppressed by the inhibitor sitting in the denominator — the "local excitation" the heading names. The inhibitor is produced wherever the activator is present, through the $k_i a^2$ term. For the mechanism this heading points at ("global inhibition") to work, the inhibitor has to spread and act over a longer range than the activator does — a comparison of $D_a$ and $D_i$ that this file does not carry out with numbers. ## Dimensionless form The notes rescale the four variables — "choose dimensionless variable $\to$ normalize 4 variables" — into dimensionless activator $A$, inhibitor $I$, position $s$, and time $\tau$. The specific substitution is not given in this material, only the result: $$\frac{\partial A}{\partial \tau} = 1 + R\frac{A^2}{I} - A + \frac{\partial^2 A}{\partial s^2}, \qquad \frac{\partial I}{\partial \tau} = Q(A^2 - I) + P\frac{\partial^2 I}{\partial s^2}.$$ Three dimensionless parameters remain: $R$ and $Q$ (combinations of the original rate constants), and $P$, which multiplies the inhibitor's diffusion term while the activator's diffusion coefficient has been normalized to $1$ — so $P$ plays the role of a diffusion ratio between the two species, though the notes do not spell out its definition either. ## The homogeneous steady state A spatially uniform, time-independent solution has $\partial/\partial s = \partial/\partial \tau = 0$, which turns the two PDEs into two algebraic equations for the uniform values $\bar A, \bar I$: $$0 = 1 + R\frac{\bar A^2}{\bar I} - \bar A, \qquad 0 = Q(\bar A^2 - \bar I).$$ The second equation gives $\bar I = \bar A^2$ directly. Substituting that into the first cancels the $\bar A^2$ against $\bar I$ exactly, leaving $$1 + R - \bar A = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar A = R + 1, \qquad \bar I = (R+1)^2,$$ which matches the notes. Because the nonlinear term cancelled, what is left is linear in $\bar A$, which is exactly why the notes can say "only one fixed point, since both $A$ and $I > 0$" — a quadratic would generally allow two roots, but this one does not stay quadratic. ## Stability of the uniform state To check whether $(\bar A, \bar I)$ is stable against a perturbation that is itself still uniform, linearize the reaction terms (temporarily setting the diffusion terms aside) around the fixed point. Writing $f(A,I) = 1 + RA^2/I - A$ and $g(A,I) = Q(A^2 - I)$ for the two right-hand sides, the Jacobian is $$J = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{2RA}{I} - 1 & -\dfrac{RA^2}{I^2} \\[4pt] 2QA & -Q \end{pmatrix}.$$ Evaluating at $\bar A = R+1$, $\bar I = (R+1)^2$ (the $I$ in the first entry cancels a power of $R+1$; the $A^2/I^2$ in the second becomes $1/(R+1)^2$) gives $$J\big|_{\bar A, \bar I} = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{R-1}{R+1} & -\dfrac{R}{(R+1)^2} \\[4pt] 2(R+1)Q & -Q \end{pmatrix},$$ exactly the matrix the notes give. For a two-variable linear system, both eigenvalues of $J$ have negative real part — the fixed point is stable — exactly when $\operatorname{tr} J < 0$ and $\det J > 0$. Here $$\operatorname{tr} J = \frac{R-1}{R+1} - Q, \qquad \det J = Q,$$ so the two conditions collapse to $$\frac{R-1}{R+1} < Q, \qquad Q > 0,$$ reproducing the notes. The slide adds a further remark, given in the source as "in general: real part of eigenvalues $> 0$." That is the trace/determinant test's generalization beyond two dimensions — instability sets in exactly when some eigenvalue of the Jacobian acquires positive real part — but the material does not disambiguate whether it is restating the stability condition just derived or already looking ahead to the instability the next section goes hunting for; it sits right at the join between the two. ## Perturbing the uniform state in space The sharper question a Turing-type analysis is built around is whether a state that is stable against a *uniform* perturbation can still be destabilized by a perturbation that *varies in space*, once diffusion is allowed to act on it. Write $$A(s,\tau) = \bar A + A'(s,\tau), \qquad I(s,\tau) = \bar I + I'(s,\tau),$$ substitute into the dimensionless PDEs, and drop terms of second order and higher in $A', I'$. The reaction part linearizes to the same Jacobian as above; the diffusion terms, already linear, come along unchanged: $$\frac{\partial A'}{\partial \tau} = \frac{R-1}{R+1}A' - \frac{R}{(1+R)^2}I' + \frac{\partial^2 A'}{\partial s^2}, \qquad \frac{\partial I'}{\partial \tau} = 2Q(1+R)A' - QI' + P\frac{\partial^2 I'}{\partial s^2}.$$ To see what a spatially varying perturbation does, the notes try a single spatial mode as an ansatz, $$A'(s,\tau) = \hat A(\tau)\cos\!\left(\frac{s}{\ell}\right), \qquad I'(s,\tau) = \hat I(\tau)\cos\!\left(\frac{s}{\ell}\right),$$ with $\ell$ setting the wavelength of the trial pattern. The choice is not arbitrary: $\cos(s/\ell)$ is an eigenfunction of $\partial^2/\partial s^2$, with $\partial^2/\partial s^2 \cos(s/\ell) = -\ell^{-2}\cos(s/\ell)$, so substituting it turns every spatial derivative into a multiple of the same profile. The $\cos(s/\ell)$ factor then cancels out of both equations, and what would have been a pair of partial differential equations for $A'(s,\tau)$, $I'(s,\tau)$ collapses to an ordinary differential equation for the two amplitudes $\hat A(\tau)$, $\hat I(\tau)$ alone, with diffusion entering only as an extra $-\ell^{-2}$ (respectively $-P\ell^{-2}$) added to the two diagonal entries of the Jacobian above. That is as far as the supplied material goes. The next step — carrying out that substitution and reading off the range of $\ell$ (equivalently, the band of wavenumbers $1/\ell$) for which the amplitudes actually grow, which is the pattern-forming instability condition this whole calculation is aimed at — is not present in the file. The slide re-states the trial solution a second time and then the transcription breaks off mid-equation. ## A figure in the notes The scanned pages include one plot, on the page immediately after the trial solution is introduced. It carries no caption or axis title in the source; only its gridlines survive the conversion. Redrawn from those gridlines, it is a single smooth curve running from $(0,0)$ up to a peak near $(1.4,\ 0.01)$, back down through zero near $x \approx 2.05$, and on down to about $-0.015$ by $x \approx 2.85$, where the scanned page is cropped. ## Sources Everything above is from a single input: the slide deck for lecture 17 ("Review") of MIT OCW 8.591J *Systems Biology* (Fall 2004, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), converted to `lectures/17-notes.md`. No transcript, separate lecture notes, or exercises were supplied for this lecture. The file carries a "reconstructed by a model" banner: the source PDF has no text layer, so a model read the pages, and the file itself flags the prose as paraphrase and every equation as unverified. Consistent with that, the file is fragmentary beyond what is reproduced above — the variable and parameter list is reassembled here from a garbled markdown table in the source; the specific rescaling that turns $(a,i,x,t)$ into $(A,I,s,\tau)$ is named but not given, so it is not reproduced; and the file breaks off mid-equation right after the spatial trial solution is introduced a second time, before the calculation is carried through to an instability condition. The one extracted figure (page 25) is unlabeled and uncaptioned in the conversion; the reading offered for it here is flagged as inference in its own caption. Being a review lecture, the file also presumes an earlier lecture's treatment of this same reaction-diffusion setup and its linear stability, which is not among the inputs supplied for this chapter.
